segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the first covenant had its requirements for worship and its sanctuary, an earthly one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For a tent was set up, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the setting out of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Behind the second curtain was a tent called the Holy of Holies,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which had a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold. In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and above it were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the place of atonement. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With these things set up in this way, the priests go continually into the first tent, carrying out their acts of worship,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins the people have committed in ignorance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By this the Holy Spirit makes clear that the way into the sanctuary has not yet been revealed while the first tent is still standing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That tent is a symbol for the present time, and in keeping with it gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshiper perfect in conscience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They deal only with foods and drinks and various washings—requirements for the flesh, imposed until the time when things are set right.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when Christ arrived as high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent—not made by hands, that is, not of this creation—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, he entered the sanctuary once for all and secured eternal redemption.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, make them holy so that their flesh is clean,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works so that we may serve the living God!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who have been called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has taken place for redemption from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For where there is a will, the death of the one who made it has to be established;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a will becomes valid only at death, since it is never in force while the one who made it is alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when Moses had spoken every commandment in accordance with the Law to all the people, he took the blood of the calves, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the scroll itself and all the people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels of the ministry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, according to the Law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it was necessary for the copies of the things in the heavens to be cleansed by these means, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by hands, a counterpart of the true one, but heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nor did he enter to offer himself many times, as the high priest enters the sanctuary year after year with blood that is not his own,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for then he would have had to suffer many times since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has been revealed once, at the end of the ages, to do away with sin by his sacrifice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will be seen a second time, apart from sin, by those who eagerly await him, for salvation.

notes.note: Elsewhere this translation renders the word “righteous requirement,” but here and in verse 10 it means a prescribed rule for the conduct of worship, with no stress on rightness. “Righteous requirements for the flesh” in verse 10 would mislead, so the adjective is dropped while “requirements” keeps the link to the word’s other uses. Most translations have “regulations” or “ordinances.”

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel’s portable wilderness sanctuary. “Tabernacle,” the older English rendering, now sounds like a special religious object and hides the plain image; several modern translations also use “tent” in Hebrews. In this passage the author calls each of the sanctuary’s two rooms a “tent.”

notes.phrase: the setting out of the loaves
notes.traditional: the showbread; the bread of the Presence
notes.note: The Greek says literally “the setting out of the loaves,” the Greek Old Testament’s expression for the twelve loaves laid out before God each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). “Showbread” and “bread of the Presence” are the traditional English names, the latter reflecting the Hebrew rather than the Greek.

notes.traditional: golden censer; golden altar of incense
notes.note: The word can mean either a censer or an incense altar; most modern translations choose the altar. In Exodus the incense altar stood in front of the curtain, not behind it. The author may link it with the inner room because of its role in the Day of Atonement rite, but the point is debated.

In the Greek Old Testament this word names the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The traditional “mercy seat” suggests a chair; “place of atonement” says what the object was for. The same phrase is used for this word in Romans 3:25, where its exact sense is disputed.

This refers to the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when the high priest entered the inner room with the blood of a bull for himself and of a goat for the people. That yearly rite is the pattern behind the argument of the whole chapter.

notes.traditional: the holiest of all; the holy places; the sanctuary
notes.note: The Greek is a plural, literally “the holy places” or “the holy things.” The same word is the name of the outer room in verse 2, but here and in verses 12, 24 and 25 it denotes the inner place of God’s presence, so “sanctuary” is used. “The first tent” in this verse may mean the outer room, as in verses 2 and 6, or the whole earthly tent as the sanctuary of the first covenant; the wording leaves both open.

notes.phrase: the good things that have come
notes.note: Some early manuscripts read “the good things that have come”; many others read “the good things to come.” The SBLGNT and most recent editions and translations follow the former, while the KJV and some others follow the latter.

The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “make holy” keeps that link visible. “Sanctify,” used by most traditional versions, means the same but now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement, which is not the point here. The reference is to ritual cleansing, including the ashes of the red heifer in Numbers 19.

The Greek has no article (“through eternal spirit”). Most interpreters and translations take this as the Holy Spirit. Others understand Christ’s own eternal spirit or nature, in contrast to the perishable animals of the old sacrifices.

The same Greek word is translated “covenant” in verses 15 and 18–20 and “will” here and in verse 17. In everyday Greek it meant a last will and testament, while the Greek Old Testament used it for God’s covenant. Most translators hold that the author plays on both senses, helped by “inheritance” in verse 15. A minority keep “covenant” throughout, taking the death to be that of the sacrificial animals that stood for the covenant-maker when a covenant was ratified.

notes.traditional: the blood of calves and goats
notes.note: Many manuscripts read “the blood of the calves and the goats,” and most English translations follow them. The SBLGNT prints the shorter reading, on the view that the longer one is an expansion influenced by verse 12. The question remains open.

notes.traditional: without sin; not to deal with sin
notes.note: The phrase is literally “without sin.” It does not contrast a sinless second coming with a sinful first. It means that the second appearing has nothing to do with dealing with sin, which was done once. Many translations paraphrase as “not to deal with sin.” The closing “for salvation” may go with “will be seen” or with “await him.”

candidates.reason: Recurs across the New Testament and shifts between “covenant” and “will/testament” here and in Galatians 3, so one policy on when to switch is needed.
The noun of the registered verb λατρεύω (“serve”); translators divide between “service” and “worship” (Romans 9:4; 12:1; John 16:2) and the noun should be aligned with the verb.
Used here for the outward, bodily sphere of ritual and not for sinful nature; versions vary between “flesh” and “body” and the choice should be consistent with Paul’s usage.

Frequent across John, Paul and Hebrews and rendered variously “reveal,” “appear,” “make manifest,” “disclose,” and needs to be kept distinct from ἀποκαλύπτω and from the other “appear” verbs in verses 24 and 28.
With λύτρωσις (v. 12) and λύτρον it forms a word-family where “redemption,” “ransom,” “release” and “liberation” compete, and readers should see the family rendered consistently.
